summary:
Eastern Visayas, six provinces in the eastern central Philippines, stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which applies uniformly across the region. The sources record no regional deviation from that framework and no anti-discrimination ordinance in force within the region's six provinces.

Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex marriage is not recognised: the Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman. Legal gender recognition is unavailable. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A trans visitor therefore presents documents that continue to show their birth-assigned sex.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. Legislation filed in Congress since 1999 has not been enacted, and the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending since the 2000s. Protections take the form of local ordinances at barangay, city, municipal and provincial level elsewhere in the country, alongside sectoral statutes: the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment, the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic and homophobic slurs with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar, and Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

None of the eight provinces recorded as having a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance, namely Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, lies in Eastern Visayas, and the 32 cities and municipalities with such ordinances are not recorded as being in the region. A visitor to the six provinces can therefore expect national statute and national practice to govern any complaint, with no regional ordinance layer to draw on.

Public attitudes remain constrained. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, so facility access in the region should be approached with the same caution the national figures imply. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

State protection machinery exists on paper without delivery at national level. Executive Order 100 s.2019, signed on 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 s.2023 added a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025. The Commission on Human Rights has described a pattern of transfemicide in the country's killings of trans people that year.

Detention would follow national practice rather than any regional rule. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, with no gender-matched placement; the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's practice of transferring LGBT detainees to a separate annex, recorded in Davao, is administrative segregation rather than recognition of gender identity. The sources do not describe the jails of the six provinces.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally and recent, which sets the baseline expectation for the region. The sources record no trans-specific killing inside Eastern Visayas itself.
tangentialFactors:
The national violence picture is the context a visitor carries into the region. On 23 June 2025 the 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province, after being reported missing on 22 June; her mother had reported the disappearance to local police. The killing occurred in the Cagayan Valley region, not Eastern Visayas, and the chairperson of the national LGBT alliance Bahaghari called it part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill.

Other documented attacks sit outside the region as well: in June 2025 a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in General Santos, in May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the equality bill.

Local ordinances elsewhere in the country restrict gender presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. No equivalent ordinance is recorded for Eastern Visayas, but neither is any ordinance shielding gender-diverse people there.

Comparative placement matters: the region sits below a national position that is scored at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 62 for trans travellers, in the 'Exercise Caution' band, with 81 for HIV-positive travellers. The absence of a regional ordinance layer places Eastern Visayas among the parts of the country where the national baseline is the whole of the legal environment.

Visibility is high nationally. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events, LGBTQ+ nightlife and media presence, openly gay and bisexual people have served in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017 with uniform policy following the legal gender on the birth certificate, and the lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card allowing registered LGBTQ couples to make medical decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.
localsOnly:
Eastern Visayas shows local LGBTQ political participation without any legal deviation from the national position. In Northern Samar, two of the province's 24 municipalities were reported around 2012 to be run by openly LGBTQ mayors, and Leyte is among the provinces listed as having LGBTQ elected officials.

Residents of the six provinces have no administrative route to change the sex marker on a birth certificate; the Clerical Error Law forecloses it and a court order remains the only avenue, with the 2008 Supreme Court ruling holding that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female such as X or non-binary, but it had not been enacted as of the reports.

Residents cannot marry a same-sex partner, and no regional ordinance provides a discrimination complaint mechanism. Protection depends on national sectoral statutes, including the Magna Carta of Women, the Safe Spaces Act, Republic Act 11166 on HIV and SOGIE discrimination, and the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers, together with any barangay, city or municipal ordinance actually adopted by an individual local government unit in the region.

National equality machinery has not been operationalised: the Diversity and Inclusion Program created by Executive Order 100 s.2019 and the special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee added by Executive Order 51 s.2023 were neither implemented as of 2025. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress since the 2000s, and national legislation on the subject has gone unenacted since 1999.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any local government unit within Eastern Visayas has adopted a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance is unresolved. The sources enumerate ordinances elsewhere in the country without giving a complete list of the 32 cities and municipalities concerned, so the absence of a named Eastern Visayas ordinance in the inventory is not proof that none exists.

The support and facilities figures come from a 2018 national Social Weather Stations survey and are not broken down for the region; whether attitudes in the six provinces diverge from the national numbers is not sourced. The national travel-risk scores likewise describe Manila rather than Eastern Visayas, and no city-level score for the region is available.

The Northern Samar figure of two openly LGBTQ mayors in 24 municipalities dates from around 2012 and is single-sourced to an online encyclopaedia; current office-holders in those municipalities are not sourced, and the Leyte reference to elected officials is unspecific as to names, dates and offices.

The status of Executive Order 100 s.2019 and Executive Order 51 s.2023 as unimplemented is stated as of 2025 in a country overview updated on 12 March 2026, so later administrative action is not excluded.

No source in the inventory describes policing, detention conditions, HIV and transition-related healthcare access, or documented violence against trans people inside Eastern Visayas itself. The killing of Kierra Apostol and the other violent incidents cited belong to other regions of the country and are carried as national-climate evidence only.
